html:
A busy day, starting with that traditional fixture: visiting the family graves.

I told my childhood friend we were going to the graves today, and he said it’s a must on the program for anyone coming back to K.

The last time I visited the graves was when I came home last April, to see Grandma, Mom’s mother, who died in 2020. The last time I did it in winter, out in the deep snow, was at least ten years ago.

The children of my eldest aunt on Mom’s side had sent Mom money and asked us to burn some offerings for them too: joss paper, paper money for the dead. So since last night my parents had been trying to line up a car, one that could hold a lot of bundles of paper. It didn’t work out: the big vehicles had room for only two passengers, and the small cars couldn’t take that much paper. So Mom decided to hire two cars, and the problem was solved, as problems so often are, with money. This morning Second Aunt, one of Dad’s sisters, led us to a shop near her place that sells it at 7.5 yuan a bundle. Thirty packs of yellow paper, several bags of paper gold ingots, banknotes in hundred-million-yuan denominations: we filled one taxi’s trunk, back seat and front passenger seat, and then the trunk of the other. The roads in K County are unusually slick this year. Nobody spreads de-icer anymore, and every day brings a steady run of car accidents and falls. Out in the countryside no one clears the snow from the roads, so the wheel ruts have taken over the job of sculpting it. We crept along carefully all the way to the ancestral graves of Dad’s and Mom’s families. We started with Dad’s side. Buried there are my grandfather and grandmother, my grandfather’s uncle, and one ancestor I don’t know. The snow was very deep; one careless step and it was over your ankles. Lighting the fire is the technical part of a winter grave visit. Dad and I made a human windbreak, and it took several tries before it caught. The flame emerged shyly, then spread with abandon. I quickly dropped the paper in my hand onto the ground and fed it more; in an instant the fire flared and, riding its black smoke, surged into the sky, which in a Northeast winter, when there’s no smog, is always a deep, clear blue. I opened a pack of Zhonghua, the premium Chinese cigarette brand, and tossed it into the fire; Grandma loved to smoke. With the wind fanning the flames, it all burned out in a little over ten minutes. Job done, we headed for Mom’s family graves.

Mom and Dad carrying the paper money

Just as I wrote this, my headphones, very fittingly, shuffled to “Take Me Home, Country Roads”:

Life is old there, older than the trees
Younger than the mountains, growin’ like a breeze

Country roads, take me home
To the place I belong

Beside the graves stand trees I’ve known since I was little, and not far off is E Mountain. A few hundred years old, I’d guess. For the ancestors beneath the earth, their lives really are older than those trees, and younger than the mountain.

Walking in snow takes forever, and with a headwind on top of that, the three of us moved very slowly. Mom’s family graves hold four or five ancestors too, including her parents. In April, when I came to Grandma’s grave, I cried very loudly. Even on the train from H City to K County, passing the bare black earth and the grave mounds that rose out of it every so often, I had thought of Grandma and wondered what her grave looked like. My heart grew heavy. When I came home in 2019, it was just after a serious illness, and that visit turned out to be our final goodbye. By then, after three years of the pandemic, Grandma had been at rest in the black earth for more than two years. When I reached her grave, the grief came pouring out, and I all but wailed. Afterwards I felt calm, as if something that had long weighed on me had been settled, as if I had finally said a proper goodbye to her.

Grandma is my hero. A tiny old woman who couldn’t read a single Chinese character, she raised a whole crowd of us children. I have long planned to write about her life.

This time, at her grave, I stayed calm. We burned more than twenty bundles of paper, opened another pack of Zhonghuas, and in ten-odd minutes it was over. I took a long drag on the Zhonghua in my hand, looked up at the endless white snow, and got back into the car.

After lunch, the three of us went off to another Northeast tradition: the bathhouse. We had held off bathing so that we could visit the graves once the weather warmed up a little and bathe afterwards, so by now we were all desperate for it. Shower, steam, scrub-down, wash, sauna, nap, wash again: by the time we had done the full circuit it was half past three. Dad said not many people go to the bathhouse these days, fewer even than during the pandemic. That matched what a taxi driver in H City told me: business this year is no better than during the pandemic, even with all the “little southern potatoes” coming up, as Harbin nicknamed the tourists from southern China who flooded the city this winter. In 2023–2024, nobody has much money in their pockets. After all that “pooling our strength to accomplish great things,” as the official slogan goes, who has much left over?

Back home, Mom said: “If you two are going to your Third Aunt’s, why not go today? Then it won’t be hanging over you before New Year.” That morning Dad had told her he wanted to take me to see Third Aunt, and Mom had said, “Go. Everyone’s getting on in years now. Nobody can promise nothing will happen. Don’t leave yourselves with regrets.” We bought two cases of beer, a case of canned fruit and a case of canned eight-treasure porridge, and headed off to the village again. Third Aunt’s husband was home; she was out playing mahjong. We made small talk. Her granddaughter is in her second year at university, her 15-year-old grandson is taller than me, she has had new teeth put in and looks different, and I still don’t have a kid. Third Aunt asked me, “What’s your mom up to?” I said, “She’s at home.”

By custom, when you visit relatives in the countryside, you don’t leave empty-handed. So we came away with three heads of suancai, the Northeast’s pickled cabbage, a bag of potatoes and a small basket of local eggs. The whole visit took about fifteen minutes; then we said goodbye and left with our bags, the taxi still waiting outside. The car stereo played the same song over and over, a Mandopop ballad called “Loving Someone Is So Hard.” I told the driver the song must be at least 22 or 23 years old; I loved it in middle school. He laughed: “Songs these days, I can’t make sense of them.”

I just looked it up: the song came out in 1999, so I undersold it by a few years.
